articles.summary: O levantamento de preços da Black Friday revela descontos de até 27% em TVs e eletrodomésticos, mas alerta que 25 dos 74 itens pesquisados estão acima da média.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Para checar se os preços da Black Friday , nesta sexta (27), têm descontos de verdade, o Guia de Compras pesquisou na última semana como estão os preços de 74 produtos.

No dia da Black Friday, 43 itens ficaram com preços abaixo da média calculada para o período – ou 58% do total. Na quinta (26), eram 45 itens com desconto.

É o segundo maior índice de produtos com valores mais baratos desde o início da varredura diária, na quinta-feira passada (19). O levantamento começou a ser feito em agosto.

Nesta semana, alguns itens chegaram a ficar até duas vezes mais caros em apenas 24 horas.

A alta de descontos é puxada principalmente pelos produtos da marca de eletrodomésticos Hisense , que repetiu o desempenho da quinta (26) e manteve 4 dos seus itens entre os 5 mais baratos.

Veja os produtos com os maiores descontos registrados no início da madrugada de sexta-feira:

TV Hisense Hi-QLED 100Q7QG 100" : 27% abaixo da média (R$ 9.999);

Lava e seca Hisense Serie 3s 12kg/8kg WD3S1243BB1 : 19% abaixo da média (R$ 2.548);

Micro-ondas Panasonic 21L NN-ST27LWRU : 16% abaixo da média (R$ 417);

TV Hisense QLED 55Q7QGPTOBT 55" : 15% abaixo da média (R$ 1.999);

Os valores são referentes ao preço no cartão e não consideram descontos no Pix.

O Guia de Compras vai registrar mais uma varredura de preços no final da manhã de sexta , para verificar se os valores mudaram.

A lista completa com os descontos está na página especial do Guia de Compras.

No total, 13 produtos tiveram quedas a partir de 10% em relação à média do período. A maioria, no entanto, continua com descontos tímidos: 18 itens ficaram abaixo dos 5%.

Por outro lado, 25 dos 74 itens estão mais caros do que a média desde agosto. Da lista, 18 itens tiveram alta entre 1% e 9%, e outros 7, acima de 10%.

É aí que mora o risco: se um produto sobe agora e cai na Black Friday, o “desconto” pode só devolvê-lo ao preço de antes.

É o terceiro ano seguido em que o Guia de Compras faz o levantamento, com base em buscas regulares nas principais lojas da internet. A lista inclui as categorias mais procuradas nesta época, como celulares, TVs, eletrodomésticos, eletroportáteis e videogames.

Como usar o comparador de preços do Guia de Compras?

Na página inicial, você pode visualizar o produto pela faixa de desconto (5%, 10%, 15%) ou selecionar a categoria desejada (ex: Cozinha).

Escolha o modelo do produto em que você procura.

Na página do item, um gráfico de variação de preços mostra rapidamente os momentos em que o produto esteve mais caro e as datas em que atingiu os menores valores.

Também é possível consultar uma tabela completa com todas as cotações registradas entre agosto e o momento atual.

articles.title: Inside “Avengers: Doomsday”, Marvel’s ‘most ambitious project we’ve ever attempted’
articles.summary: Twenty-two faces from the MCU pull back the curtain on the epic multiverse mash-up.
articles.body:
Expectations are running high the Saturday morning of July's San Diego Comic-Con. The sounds from the lobby of the Pendry Hotel, just a few cobblestoned blocks away from the main convention arena, are deafening due to cross-chatter from scores of fans and industry insiders — all wearing colorful Star Trek lanyards that bear their entry passes, some carrying the free swag bags now stuffed with merch.

It's the biggest day of one of the biggest geekified conventions of the year, made grander because of the presence of Marvel . Behind the scenes ahead of their big Hall H presentation, Marvel filmmaking veteran Joe Russo remarks, "It's a production, independent of the film."

A year earlier at the same pop culture stage, the Hollywood studio behind the mightiest of heroes announced that Joe and his brother, Anthony Russo — the directors behind some of the studio's biggest movies, including Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame — would return to the House of M to take on the next two Avengers entries, subtitled Doomsday (in theaters Dec. 18) and Secret Wars (Dec. 17, 2027).

Joining them would be Robert Downey Jr. , returning to the fold six years after the death of his beloved character, Tony Stark, to now play the villain of both films, "Doctor" Victor von Doom.

To the fans on the ground, it felt like the perfect way for Marvel to bounce back after a widely discussed string of box office stumbles that forced the studio to rethink its release strategy, ultimately trimming the number of films and shows rolled out within a 12-month span. And a year later, at Comic-Con 2026, it was finally time to pull back the curtain and show everyone what they'd been working on.

On this Saturday, all that separates 15 stars of Avengers: Doomsday from the awaiting fans in the Pendry lobby — some of whom will later try to verbally fight their way through security to get into the past-capacity Marvel presentation in Hall H — is an actual curtain.

Beyond a black floor-to-ceiling enclosure inside the second-floor ballroom, swarms of black-clad security guards, publicists, and individual squadrons of hair-and-makeup and wardrobe stylists attend to the ensemble. Chris Evans, Hayley Atwell, Paul Rudd, Anthony Mackie, Danny Ramirez, Simu Liu, James Marsden, Kelsey Grammer, David Harbour, Lewis Pullman, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke, Hannah John-Kamen, and Tenoch Huerta Mejia are all present for Entertainment Weekly 's cover shoot, directed by the Russos themselves.

One of the few stars absent today is Rebecca Romijn , reprising her role as Mystique from the long-lost age of live-action X-Men movies. She'll explain to EW a few months later that she was "running back and forth doing double duty" with Star Trek: Strange New Worlds . "It was pretty exciting, and I've never been more exhausted in my life."

For most of the actors, including Pedro Pascal , Doomsday marks their first Avengers film.

"It's the biggest ensemble I've ever been a part of," the man behind the stretchable leader of the Fantastic Four, one of the few cast members who will be filmed separately and digitally inserted into the final motion cover, comments on the assemblage. "To put us all in a room together, you would expect it to feel atomic. And yet it was like [an] immediate family. It was really warm. No one was alone, that was for sure."

Despite starring in four prior Avengers blockbusters as an actual god, Chris Hemsworth admits he felt like "the odd one out" among this swath of Marvel's next gen. "Being on set and now feeling like one of the elder statesmen, or one of the elders, was oddly uncomfortable at first," the Thor actor says. "Then I was having that conversation [with] Chris Evans and the Russos. What it led to is, well, no, we are experienced. We started this journey over a decade ago."

Downey holds court as the most seasoned MCU star in the ballroom, which is decked out to look like Doom's Latverian throne room. Donning a green blazer, black T-shirt, and gold chain around his neck, he stands at the epicenter of this swirl of bodies, clutching his metallic mask as costars rehearse their blocking. He seems content to keep up the energy of the entire room, silently screaming and flashing devil horns at the camera, all while rocking his body to the soundtrack playing in his head.

Later in the day, he brings up memories of his first Comic-Con in 2007, when he joined Gwyneth Paltrow, Jon Favreau, and Terrence Howard to promote the first Iron Man , the film that kicked off decades of storytelling. "I think about what all of my co-heroes here have had to do to pull their own weight and keep fans interested," Downey says. "It seemed like [Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige ] had this idea: What if we just really do what our brand is and do something unexpected that gives everyone a reason to reconvene?"

After Avengers: Endgame , which concluded Marvel's boldest cross-film narrative to date in 2019, everyone seemed content to head into Marvel retirement. At least publicly. The Russos keep it succinct. "We were tired," Joe says of he and his brother after making four large-scale movies, including Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014) and Captain America: Civil War (2016), over several years. "It was exhausting," he adds, "and we needed some space and some time to process."

The same goes for Evans, the man behind Steve Rogers, who we saw in Endgame pass his Captain America shield on to Mackie's Sam Wilson and go off into another timeline to grow old with his true love, Atwell's Peggy Carter. Despite what he told the press — that he was " happily retired " and " sad to not be back with the band " — Evans took multiple meetings with Marvel in secret in the years following Endgame .

"He's very committed to saving the experience for the movie theater," Anthony Russo remarks of his star's misleading comments. "He's like, 'Why would we ever compromise that?' Of anybody involved, as far as the cast goes, he may be the most committed to that aspect."

While filming Endgame , Lou D'Esposito (co-president, Marvel Studios) and Kevin Feige took Evans to dinner. "They said, 'We'd love to continue making movies with you. Steve would no longer be Captain America, he would be Nomad,'" the actor recalls — Nomad being Steve's post-Cap man-without-a-country persona from the comics. "They sent me a pitch and it was a great pitch. It really was. But for whatever reason at the time, I was very happy with how things wrapped up. It didn't feel like it was the thing I was looking to do at the time."

The Russos' experience was similar. With Endgame , they wanted to "leave it all on the floor," Anthony says. Yet, Joe notes, "If the timing was right, the story was right, we'd do it again." As the years went by, they routinely questioned whether that time had arrived, all because of one comic book event they still wanted to tackle: Secret Wars .

The first Marvel Comics arc to bear that name — the one that kicked off in 1984 from writer Jim Shooter and artist duo Mike Zeck and Bob Layton — told of a cosmic entity called the Beyonder, who snatched various heroes and villains from across the Marvel world and put them all together on a Hunger Games -style planet called Battleworld to see who would become the victor.

The second and far more recent Secret Wars of 2015 — written by Jonathan Hickman with art from Esad Ribić and covers by Alex Ross — began with a series of "incursions," in which different worlds collide into each other. From the rubble emerges Battleworld, a Play-Doh mash-up of parts from each reality. No matter the iteration, Doctor Doom was a major player.

If you ask Feige, the MCU's version of the Secret Wars storyline will lean far more heavily into Hickman's run, including the "Time Runs Out" prelude issues to the main event. If you ask the Russos, however, it's "a little bit of both" runs and not a strict one-to-one adaptation, either.

"We had been talking about it for years on and off," Anthony says, "but we could never really turn the corner on why ." Then came an idea from the filmmakers' screenwriting collaborator, Stephen McFeely. The pitch, which the brothers call their "light bulb," became a featured scene in this year's theatrical Avengers: Endgame re-release : Steve Rogers reunites with Peggy Carter, the same as we remember from the end of the movie, but now the camera lingers just a few moments longer to show Loki (Tom Hiddleston) arrive at their doorstep with a warning.

It was a "risky" play, Joe acknowledges. "There's part of us that didn't want to mess with the movie that everybody knew and loved, and that we love as is," Anthony elaborates. "But we felt it was acceptable for us as filmmakers, our taste, in terms of what we wanna see on the screen and the expression we wanna make. We were okay with going one tiny step past what you knew as the ending of that movie. And in that tiny step, things significantly change in ways we couldn't have expected back when we made the movie."

Atwell, who says she was "sitting there, hoping I'd get the call" to return, calls Cap and Peggy's love story "a beating heart to this installment," adding, "It felt really special that it would have a moment again."

Like one reality timestream branching out into multiple, everything that came next seemed to stem from that moment, including the return of the X-Men and reintroducing Downey to the MCU as Doom. "Joe called and he pitched the big idea," Evans remembers. "I said, 'Now that's interesting. That's something that I could take a risk on.'"

This big idea now feels more grand than even Endgame . If that film was billed as a culmination of 11 years of Marvel storytelling, then the one-two punch of Doomsday and Secret Wars marks a bigger climax.

"By far and away the most ambitious project we've ever attempted is the convergence of 25 years of storytelling, all the way back to the first X-Men in 2000," Joe says. "It's three major franchises crashing into each other. So the real work was around trying to give each group a collective arc that the audience could follow and root for them."

The story of Avengers: Doomsday has been relayed piecemeal through the post-credits scenes and trailers leading up to this moment.

The multiverse is collapsing. A series of incursions causes different realities to collide into one another. With only a few remaining, the main world of the Avengers, the world of the Fantastic Four, and the world of the X-Men will bleed into each other, mixing all their colorful personalities.

The kingdom of Wakanda, now ruled by M'Baku (Winston Duke), will cross paths with Sue Storm (Vanessa Kirby) and her Fantastic family of heroes. "Being king is great," Duke comments. "However it evolves [from here] is fantastic and we're just excited to bring something new for the fans that are on the other side of the screen." As for Shuri, "She's grown, she's developed, she's more mature, and she's anchored in the position that she's taken up," explains Letitia Wright , whose character assumed the mantle of Black Panther. "You see it in the suit, you see in the swagger, you see in how she carries herself."

Meanwhile, the squad formerly known as the Thunderbolts are actively competing with Sam Wilson to establish themselves as the de facto Avengers. "We're there to bring our neuroses and our problems and our depression right to Captain America or Ant-Man," David Harbour (Alexei Shostakov/Red Guardian) affirms.

"We just finished Thunderbolts* and then I think the next day we were straight [into] Avengers ," Hannah John-Kamen (Ava Starr/Ghost) says. "I didn't take my suit off, basically. I slept in it and then turned up."

These main sets of heroes will collide to face Doctor Doom, the next post-Thanos big bad. But so many other details remain, erm, secret on purpose. For one, what exactly is the story the Russos are telling with this movie? Sure, there are incursions and reality-crossing characters, but if The Winter Soldier was a political thriller and most of Endgame was a heist movie across time, what is Doomsday ?

"That's a challenging question," Anthony admits, acknowledging they don't want to overreach into spoiler terrain.

Joe speaks about it only in a thematic sense. "All our films are really about the same moment," he explains. "It's when somebody that you love makes a choice that you can't forgive. What happens after that moment? I think Doomsday is maybe the best expression of that theme that we've been playing with for our entire careers."

According to Feige, Doom was on his mind well before Marvel parted ways with actor Jonathan Majors , who was originally going to anchor the film as the villain Kang the Conqueror, back when Doomsday was called Avengers: Kang Dynasty . Majors' guilty verdict in a domestic dispute certainly contributed to the studio's decision to bring in Doom, "but that wasn't the only part of it," Feige insists.

"People who know the Secret Wars comic books know Doom is a huge part of that," he explains. "So we were always leaning towards Secret Wars , but knew that there was no way to do that without bringing in Doctor Doom. We really were talking about building it in even the earliest of Kang Dynasty stories. That movie led to Doom. And then when the story shifted, it just became more and more and more Doom-focused because we wanted to earn him and build him into the Secret Wars storyline."

Victor hails from the same universe as Reed Richards (Pascal), Sue Storm (Kirby), Johnny Storm (Joseph Quinn), and Ben Grimm (Ebon Moss-Bachrach), who all debuted in The Fantastic Four: First Steps (2025). That connection mirrors the long history these characters share in Marvel Comics, wherein Doom typically serves as the storied archvillain opposite the heroic quartet.

The Marvel team "discussed a few different places" for Doom in the MCU, Feige shares, but not in First Steps beyond the post-credits scene. He reasons, "There had been so many other Fantastic Four films with Doctor Doom in it." Those include actor Joseph Culp's Doom in 1994's low-budget Fantastic Four , Julian McMahon in the 2000s duology (which featured a pre-Captain America Evans as the Human Torch), and Toby Kebbell in the 2015 reboot.

The new Doom has an established relationship with the MCU's Fantastic Four, particularly Reed. In their youth, Victor and the man who would grow up to become Mr. Fantastic were close friends at university. "The love and respect that Doom and Reed have for each other in Doomsday is critical to the storytelling," Joe says.

The same goes for the actors playing them. Downey, who recently swapped Marvel personas with Pascal for their Halloween costumes, says, "We are the guys that always pick up each other's FaceTimes, because we literally have just become a new version of science bros," Downey comments.

The punk-rock performances of Downey's earlier work imprinted on Pascal in his youth. The Mandalorian star shouts out 1985's Tuff Turf and Weird Science . "He's way, way, way up there for somebody that I would call when I need to hear advice from a friend," Pascal remarks.

Maybe that's how Reed and Victor would describe their relationship in school. But now, as Pascal frames their connection, "Reed struggled to use his power of intelligence and understanding of science for the good of his family and the good of mankind, whereas Doom, with equal, if not superior intellectual power, uses it for questionable attainment of power. There's so much delicious conflict there standing on other ends of the spectrum."

Sue — who's "more cautious about Doom" without Reed's blind spots, Joe says — relays some of that history in Avengers: Doomsday , which introduces Doom now in the present as a formidable sorcerer from the nation of Latveria.

The Russos gravitated toward the character's relationship with the occult. Suffering a tragic loss, Victor turned to "a very dark and ancient magic," Joe shares. "Everything in his world extends from that.

That includes the Latverian witches, three mysterious masked figures donning different-colored robes that act as Doom's coven. Little is known about them, though Marvel disclosed their existence in promotional materials.

Fans, for sure, have their theories, one of which posits Wanda Maximoff could be under one of the masks. In the weeks since completing interviews for this cover story, a lot more has been revealed in the MCU, including the resurrection of Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch by Doom in a VisionQuest ending tag. (The Russos declined to comment when asked in a follow-up email.)

Joe only gives this mild tease: "His relationship to that dark magic and the witches are an extension of that world [of Latveria]. They do have a history that is from the books and [a history] that is a surprise."

The occult nature of Doom lends to heavier material. While there will always be the sense of humor expected from the Disney-owned brand, Downey describes the story as "pretty dark" and Anthony Russo points to the "shades of horror" that come through. "Doom is a dark figure," the director continues. "He's a wounded figure. He's a figure that has worked very hard to protect himself from vulnerabilities that he's experienced. There's a relentlessness with which he's approaching that."

"This is a guy who is vengeful and capable of doing things, because he's lost so much that to lose this [battle] would be for all to be lost," explains Downey, who says he tapped into "a scorched-earth vibe." And yet, "vengeful," he adds, "doesn't quite go deep enough."

The Oppenheimer Oscar winner channels what he calls a "really crabbed [Neil] deGrasse Tyson" when he says, "The mechanics that have made every previous Marvel film possible are really what he seeks revenge against. It's literally like I have contempt for the cosmos as it has been rendered."

Downey admits that Doom is "one of the most technical things I'll ever have to do." To build the character, he first turned to Nate Merritt, a graphic designer and long-time creative consultant on his personal team, to draw storyboards and keyframe art to chronicle the origins of Doom. (Merritt's been "NDA'd within an inch of his life," Downey jests.)

The actor wanted "something visual to lean into." He approached Stark the same way; an image of Iron Man tinkering away in his workshop with various armor pieces adorning his body became his anchor. With Doom, Downey wanted to move as far away from Stark as possible — "considering that I, on occasion, have trouble differentiating myself from Tony to begin with," he says.

Of course, to talk about Downey's Doom is to broach the subject of lookalikes. Because of Downey's history in the MCU, Doom will now strangely resemble Stark, whom many of the OG Avengers still grieve. In a franchise where there are "variants" of characters from different dimensions played by the same actors, the obvious question is whether Doom is a variant of Tony. Feige came out recently to declare "no." The Russos are a bit more coy: "You'll have to watch the movie."

It's still a bold swing to bring back the actor who began this entire 38-film, 18-show franchise (and counting) to play one of the most recognizable villains in all of Marvel canon. As Feige once put it , "It's our universe. It's a multiverse. We can do whatever the heck we want. He played the most iconic hero. Let's have him play the most iconic villain."

Hemsworth describes working with Downey now as Doom, after so many years of Stark, as "oddly unsettling, in the best way."

"All of a sudden, he's entirely twisted and transformed into something else," the actor says. "That's not Iron Man, that's not Tony Stark, that's not even Robert Downey."

It plays into Hemsworth's approach to the Asgardian god of thunder. "There's a strange, hypnotic familiarity there for Thor," he says of Doom, "but there's an uncertainty and a hesitation and a mistrust."

The moment the Russos felt like Doom was in the room with them was the first time Downey turned on the accent. "It wasn't on set," Joe recalls. "It was in his trailer and we were going over lines with him. We were like, 'There it is! There's the character.'"

They could just feel it. "It's like him trying out different bicycles to see which one fits the best," Joe continues. "He had been trying out different accents. He slipped into this [one] and it added a color and a texture."

Downey considers Doom in relation to Stark. "I wanna go quadruple-meta," he begins. It has more to do with the audience's memory of him playing Iron Man than the characters themselves.

"Let's venture a guess and say most people know [I played Tony], then we're really talking about shadows and reflections and symbiotic separateness," he muses. "Every one of us is Tony and Victor. That's the real big top line thing here for me. And yet, I couldn't really reach out to Tony because I didn't want to tread that ground. I really wanted it to feel like, even if I hadn't ever played Stark, that Von Doom had been correctly rendered."

Feige had been thinking about introducing Doom into the MCU since the splashy Hollywood deal that saw the Walt Disney Company absorb 21st Century Fox — and with it the rights to characters including the Fantastic Four and Daredevil — in an industry-rumbling studio acquisition.

But the deal also got his brain churning about another set of characters to which he previously didn't have access: Marvel's merry band of mutants.

The X-Men hold a special place in Feige's heart. He got his start in the superhero biz behind the scenes of that first X-film (2000), which introduced the late Patrick Stewart as wheelchair-bound telepath Professor Charles Xavier, Hugh Jackman as adamantium-clawed Wolverine, Famke Janssen as red-haired telekinetic Jean Grey, James Marsden as optic-blasting Cyclops, and more.

"I vaguely remember how sweet he was," Rebecca Romijn, playing Magneto's favorite shapeshifting henchwoman Mystique, says of meeting Feige as an associate producer under Lauren Shuler Donner, a primary architect behind the X-Men movies. The actress describes Donner as "a really genuinely wonderful person," saying, "I don't doubt that she surrounds herself with also genuinely wonderful people. And that's how I feel about Kevin Feige."

Feige believed the X-Men were in his past, because of who owned the rights. "That was emotional, because I love those characters," he says. "[I] really put them aside to focus on the Marvel universe that we did have the rights to."

Then came the big studio merger. To everyone else involved in that corporate deal, the unchaining of these comic-book characters — which Marvel sold off to other studios before breaking big — felt like an afterthought. To Feige, however, "it was the most important aspect."

"The moment that happened," he says, "we started thinking about how best to integrate those characters. Now we're doing it in a way that pays tribute in a very big way to what has come before, which is what Doomsday is all about."

Stewart was the first X-vet to join Disney's Avengers-forward franchise as an Xavier from a parallel dimension of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022). Next came Kelsey Grammer as the blue-furred Hank McCoy/Beast in an end-credits scene to The Marvels (2023); the Frasier alum was told he received "a lot of great response from that little cameo," which prompted Marvel to invite him back for Doomsday .

Deadpool & Wolverine then brought a host of other mutants into the fold, including Ryan Reynolds as foul-mouthed Wade Wilson and Jackman's Logan. (Reynolds and Jackman both have writing credits on Avengers: Doomsday , but TBD on whether they actually appear on screen.) This year's event film now revisits more X-Men characters from the Fox era of movies, including Ian McKellen's master of magnetism Erik Lehnsherr/Magneto and Alan Cumming's teleporting fiend Kurt Wagner/Nightcrawler.

Channing Tatum, who nearly played Gambit in that previous franchise, is also thrown into the mix after debuting as Cajun card-slinger Remy LeBeau in Deadpool & Wolverine . "I didn't know how they were gonna pull it off, to be totally honest," Tatum says of his return for Doomsday . "I hadn't read the script when I had my first meeting with them. I just looked right at Joe and was like, 'How are you gonna do this, man?! I just can't even wrap my head around it.'"

Though, is this Gambit the exact same one who escaped the Void in that 2024 theatrical release? "I don't wanna give away where we start the movie," the actor responds. "I would venture to say maybe not, but I'm gonna leave it there."

Marsden wasn't expecting an X-Men reunion of this magnitude. "I didn't know whether or not to believe it at first, because there was so much chatter over however many years about doing another film and bringing them into this universe, and it never really came to fruition," he reasons. "But then, 'Hey, Kevin wants to chat with you.' You're thinking this has gotta be real. It's not just 'shoot the s----.'"

So why these X-Men in particular and not, say, Halle Berry's Storm or Anna Paquin's Rogue? The Russos decline to explain why just yet, but Joe promises the casting "was really targeted. It was really specific."

"We really do have a process where we see the entire film through each character's eyes, no matter what the size of their role is," Anthony says. "With the X-Men, we got to really deep dive and think about their histories as characters, their experiences, and how this particular moment in time was gonna affect them. There's such a rich history to them that we really do bring them to the film as if it's their movie, as well."

Romijn's first question when Feige called her up about reprising Mystique: "What's the makeup process going to be?" Playing the blue-skinned mutant in that first movie, the star, who was transitioning from modeling to acting at the time, would sit in the makeup station for seven to eight hours to become Magneto's go-to hitwoman. By her own estimates, two-thirds of her body was covered in scaly prosthetics, while the crew airbrushed the rest.

This time, Feige assured her it'd be "much easier," she says. "They had me wearing something which cut down on time in the prosthetics chair. A lot of the things that I dealt with in the first three movies I didn't have to deal with on this."

That includes the action. Romijn describes Mystique's fighting style in the original as "much more acrobatic," while the character in Doomsday embraces "a little more martial arts." (Perhaps by virtue of who Mystique shapeshifts into this time.) "There was talk of one specific fight move that we were gonna try and recreate," she says. "I don't think we ever got to it, but it's a famous one."

Adjustments were also made to her costume. Romijn's getup now incorporates a gold forehead chain and white fabric. "They now want to make all these characters much more comic-book accurate, which I can appreciate," she says.

The same goes for Marsden, who dons a classically blue-and-yellow Cyclops uniform instead of the all-black suit established in the aughts. The actor calls it "one of those pinch-me moments" to give the fans "everything that they want to see."

Even if his new visor isn't exactly practical. "It was very limited vision," Marsden admits.

When worlds indeed crash into each other and the mutants brush shoulders with the other heroes, there's an acclimation period. Early previews of the film showcase fight sequences between select Marvel heroes.

Gambit, for example, will throw punches (or energized playing cards) with Shang-Chi (Simu Liu). "To have a scene partner like Channing, who was as insistent as I was about getting to do as much of it as possible, was really critical to the success of that scene," Liu remarks.

"We'd get to be in a kung-fu movie! This is so fun," Tatum adds. "Anything is possible, literally."

The X-Men bring "a real edge and a real pop" to the movie, adds Joe Russo. "Mutants are in a constant fight for survival, which really is part of the DNA of who they are," he elaborates. "It's how they respond to that fight for survival that determines their place in the X-Men universe."

On a follow-up Zoom call in late October, Downey sports a custom deep violet cap with the letters "AD." Instead of "Anno Domini," or "the year of our Lord," he says it stands for "after Doom." "You're not gonna see this in that Dunkin' Donuts collab ," he jokes.

The phrasing feels appropriate. Beyond the merch messaging, there is a growing sense that there will be the Marvel universe as it existed before Doom and the Marvel universe that will form after. Writing in the foreword to the newly released Marvel Premier Collection edition of Hickman's Secret Wars comic, Feige referred to the story as "the end of the Marvel Universe as we know it," as well as "a new beginning," one that finished with a multiverse "rebuilt and retooled for the modern age."

He has similar plans for the MCU. Mindful of spoilers, Feige says both Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars are "passing the torch from one universe to another." He calls this December's release "a culmination of what's come before," while next year's "will very much be a launching pad for our films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU — and launching a very new era at that point."

Marvel's 2028 film slate will kick off with an untitled X-Men movie , featuring Sadie Sink as the new Jean Grey, Kit Connor as Cyclops, Christopher Abbott as Xavier, Inde Navarrette as Rogue, and more younger stars bringing different incarnations of known characters to the screen.

"The X-Men are extremely important," Feige says about the future of Marvel Studios. "You can't underestimate it. When you look at the comics, other than Avengers and Spider-Man, there's almost nothing more important. We talk about it in terms of sagas, because there's so many amazing sagas within the X-Men comics over the past 60 years. The potential to continue our film series is almost limitless now that we have access to the X-Men."

The studio has also announced a third Black Panther film and a new Ghost Rider , with three other unspecified Marvel movies slated for 2029. How will the universe pave the way so it makes sense canonically for what comes next? That's what we'll go to theaters to find out between Doomsday and Secret Wars .

The familiar question of "superhero fatigue" comes up, which remains a topic for the Reddit threads. Will theater-goers stick around for the next 20 years of Marvel storytelling, or did it peak with Endgame ? Is the age of the superhero movie over? Ask any fan on the ground in San Diego for Comic-Con in July, especially those who eagerly snatch up the free Doctor Doom mask and cape handed out at the Hall H panel, and it might sound silly to even pose such queries.

"It seems like everyone loves having conversations about something," responds Joe, who likens the situation to the Hollywood Western, a genre he argues didn't produce the hits until after it was declared dead. "Something has to feel like we're dying, and a lot of times the conversations are not anything substantial or truthful."

To his point, the trailers alone for both Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Avengers: Doomsday hit viewing records on YouTube at drop. The former is currently the highest-grossing movie of 2026.

"At no point did we ever think we could surpass the bar of [2021's] No Way Home and bringing in multiple Spider-Men," Feige says. "We just focused on what could be different and how we could focus on Peter's journey in a different emotional way. I would say it's a very similar thing with Doomsday and Secret Wars ."

If you ask the actors, "The key here is each time making it still grounded in the human experience," Hemsworth says. "I don't think there's any limit to that, or any fatigue with an audience's appetite."

"We believe in these movies with every ounce in us," Joe continues. "So all we can do is offer to audiences and see how they feel."

articles.title: Scott Caan Thought He Got a Prank Text. It Was Actually David Fincher Wanting Him in 'Cliff Booth'
articles.summary: The veteran actor reunites with Brad Pitt in the 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood' follow-up that sees him taking on manic 1970s TV star Charlie Peters, who's...
articles.body:
Scott Caan Thought He Got a Prank Text. It Was Actually David Fincher Wanting Him in ‘Cliff Booth’

[This story contains spoilers for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth .]

Getting battered with warnings about scammer calls and texts is nothing new in today's world. So when Scott Caan got a message, "Hey, David Fincher wants to meet you" for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , understandably he thought, "I'm being punked."

"I was going to write back like, 'Whoever this is, leave me alone.' I thought somebody was playing a joke on me. Yeah, sure, you're texting me to come be in a Fincher movie. Yeah, I believe that for sure," the 50-year-old actor quips when The Hollywood Reporter caught up with him over Zoom just hours before he headed out to the film's U.K. premiere earlier this month.

But it wasn't a joke. The filmmaker's producer partner, Ceán Chaffin, was reaching out about the role of Charlie Peters after Quentin Tarantino — who wrote the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel — and star Brad Pitt suggested Caan for the character.

Given that Tarantino is one of Caan's "favorite writers of all time," and he'd get to reunite with his Ocean's Eleven co-star Pitt, it was an easy yes. But then came the challenging part of taking on a character that "can seem a little crass and insane" on paper, he says, and figuring out, "How do I justify all this?"

Once Pitt's fan-favorite stuntman Cliff Booth gets entangled with Charlie, a popular yet manic 1970s TV star, he realizes he's not being hired as his stunt double, but rather as a fixer to handle a dangerous hitman situation Charlie has found himself in.

"I figure out a way to ground all of it. So none of it seems like an idea or a cliché or a character. I don't want anything to be cartoony," Caan says of how he approached his reckless, unintentionally comedic character on screen. "I want it to be real. And then I got to find a part of myself that is that wild, wild, wild guy."

But as an actor playing an actor, TV superstar Charlie Peters specifically, Caan wasn't just taking a singular role. He also had to embody all of Charlie's characters within the film's fictional shows… talk about a meta experience.

"A lot of people maybe might want to goof on the acting part of it, but David and I talked about it. My goal as Charlie Peters is to win Emmys," he explains, wanting those characters to be as "thorough and lived out and grounded" as anyone else he's portrayed.

Sounds like quite the undertaking, but Caan confesses it's "an actor's fantasy." He adds, "It's a dream to be able to play three or four different characters inside of the movie you've been wanting to make your whole life."

For any actor, Tarantino and Fincher are as high a pedigree creative team as it gets, which only adds to the pressure as a performer.

"I've been doing this for long enough where a lot of the time I go in there, and I feel like I need to help the writing or I need to help, maybe it's a young director," says Caan, who's been a fixture of the industry since the '90s. "Not in an egotistical way, but in a collaborative way." So showing up to set and knowing you're fully taken care of was a "very rare" experience for him.

It also allowed Caan to fully commit to those scenes that will likely have audiences talking for ages, such as Charlie, Cliff and talent agent Karen Crosby's (played by Elizabeth Debicki) first meeting when Cliff suggests Charlie kill a pig as a method acting exercise. Caan's character was understandably bewildered by the thought initially.

"That first scene where we're talking about the pig and he gives me that suggestion … it felt like we were doing a one-act play," the Entourage actor says with excitement in his voice. "As far as fun, and we did that scene a lot of times, I've never gone home and felt like, wow, that was… I never felt anything like that. We just did a one-act play 50 times today, and full 10-minute takes of that scene, and it's all over the place."

That was only the beginning of Cliff and Charlie's chaotic journey that would unfold across the next hour, but for one unfortunate piggy, it would soon be the end, as Charlie takes Cliff's acting advice quite literally. In a moment of symbolism, it's "really the beginning of my nervous breakdown," Caan says of his once-confident character now panicking, drenched in pig's blood towards the end.

"This scene, it has to work. If this scene doesn't work, then the Charlie journey is not complete," he explains. "So I remember being really, really, really sad all day long, just trying to stay in a really upset place, and Fincher was paying attention, and he just had me do it again and again and again until we were exhausted. It was a very memorable day of shooting."

While Cliff goes on to do Charlie's dirty work for him in the final showdown with the hitmen, Caan's character is left "having to deal with all of my demons, digging deep and sorting out all my trauma" that's got him to this point, he says.

Similar to how Charlie's storyline ends with a moment of reflection, that's also how Caan walked away from the movie, having wrapped his first collaboration with Fincher and Tarantino. "I wish we could start over right now," he admits.

The film also serves as the first major project Caan worked on following the death of his father and Hollywood icon James Caan in 2022 . Known for his intense, charismatic performances, Scott's Cliff Booth performance undoubtedly felt like a nod to his legacy.

"I think about him every day anyway, let alone when I'm going into doing something that I think that he would've appreciated, something that he would've been great in," he says of his dad.

But Caan is also working to build a Hollywood legacy of his own, one that already includes dozens of roles from energetic getaway driver Turk Malloy in the Ocean's Eleven franchise (and yes, he's "100 percent" down to reprise his role in Ocean's 14 ) to Detective Danny Williams in the Hawaii Five-0 reboot. And now, Charlie Peters in Cliff Booth and agent Nick Schaeffer in NCIS: New York .

Even with a stacked resume, Caan feels he's still not in a place in his career where he can be too picky about the opportunities that come his way, especially in an industry with a limited — and shrinking — number of jobs.

"I think we all would like to think that we're at a point in our career where we can pick and choose, but the truth of the matter is, I feel like when I was younger, I felt that way," he admits. "And as I get older and have been in the business for a long time, you're just kind of lucky to be working."

So when you get a text that Fincher wants to cast you in a film written by Tarantino, naturally it's going to feel pretty surreal, even for a veteran like Caan. Because even after decades in the business, he tells THR , "I'm just constantly trying to figure out what I want to be when I grow up, and I'm still doing that, and that's the fun of our business."

He quips with a laugh, "I'm still only in my 20s. I got a ways to go, you know what I mean?"

articles.title: Aryan Khan's rumoured girlfriend Larissa Bonesi says he is intelligent and determined, the Khans are like family to her: 'Shah Rukh Khan is the King, will be number one forever'
articles.summary: Brazilian model and actress Larissa Bonesi has described the Khan family as her own, speaking about her bond with actor Shah Rukh Khan and his son,
articles.body: Brazilian model and actress Larissa Bonesi has described the Khan family as her own, speaking about her bond with actor Shah Rukh Khan and his son, filmmaker Aryan Khan. Larissa and Aryan are often spotted together, which lead to the speculation that they are in a relationship. They have not commented on the rumours publicly.Larissa Bonesi, who moved to India 16 years ago and now considers Mumbai home, said her admiration for the Khans comes from both their achievements and who they are as people. She described their support as something that means a great deal to her and said the friendship she shares with the family goes a long way. Talking about her bonding, she told Bombay Times, "The Khans are like family. When you admire people for what they have achieved in life, have respect for them, and how they are as human beings, you kind of feel that they are family. Their support means a lot. Friendship is everything, and it is something that goes a long way.”While talking about Shah Rukh Khan, Larissa Bonesi was all praise. “He is the King. He is a legend, and he is going to be number one forever. There is so much to learn from him. It is not just about being famous or what you have achieved, but also about how you did it. He is someone you look up to,” she said in a conversation with Bombay Times.She was equally specific in her praise for Aryan Khan, who made his directorial debut with the web series The Bastards of Bollywood. “Aryan is a great person. He is intelligent and determined. Sometimes people say, ‘But he has everything.’ However, he does not care about that. He is fighting for what he wants, he is fighting for his future and for the things he believes in. He will get there because he is a very determined guy,” she said. Larissa Bonesi added that she visited the sets of Aryan’s show once and would love to be directed by him someday, saying anyone would want to work with someone that talented.While her friendships have helped her build a life in Mumbai, Larissa Bonesi acknowledged that navigating the Indian entertainment industry as a foreigner has not always been straightforward. She said there have been ups and downs, and that entering the industry from outside the country was difficult at first. Over time, she adapted to her circumstances and found acceptance from both the public and the people around her.On the professional front, Larissa Bonesi said she is looking forward to her upcoming horror film 1920: Cold Winter. She described herself as a fan of the horror genre and said the role was the kind she had been waiting for. articles.summary: Jace Cates takes Kylee house-hunting in downtown Austin on "Chris Harrison's The Vow," where the pair share their first kiss and open up about faith.
articles.body: WARNING: Spoilers from this week's episode of "The Vow" below. The fourth episode of "Chris Harrison's: The Vow" was packed with content as Jace Cates went on another date and got a visit from his loved ones. In the episode, titled "Mother Knows Best," Cates took Kylee out on their first solo date together, during which they went house-hunting with a real estate agent in downtown Austin. "I think there's some women that I'm really developing strong feelings for, and I'm excited to continue this journey with them," he said. "Today I chose Kylee. She's someone on the first night, we had a really great conversation. She's ambitious, she wants a lot out of her life, and she's so sweet and nice and super cute. I feel like we have a really great connection. I want to see if there's something deeper there." During their date, the two shared their first kiss and got to know each other better. ‘THE VOW’ STAR JACE CATES GETS EMOTIONAL OVER SEAN LOWE’S ADVICE ON FINDING THE ONE "Looking at all these beautiful homes, I wish it wasn't fantasyland," Kylee said. While speaking to Cates, Kylee shared more about her faith and revealed she previously appeared on "The Bachelor." She explained that after her time on that show, she still "believe[s] in environments like this," but noted that she got "burned." "It was never something that I thought I would put myself back in, but I say this like 110%. I'm a firm believer that this was something that God wanted me to do," she said. Back at the house, Haleigh and Audrey confronted Kylee about her faith, recalling a conversation Kylee had with Alexis in which they said she expressed discomfort about how faith-based the show actually is and that she didn't know coming into it that it would be to this extent. "I don't mess around when it comes to faith," Haleigh said in a confessional prior to the confrontation. "It's honestly, it bothers me when someone's gonna put on a show, especially with prayer. That's not something I take lightly. I don't look at her the same. We're gonna confront her about it." They seemed to get to a place of understanding, but Kylee left the conversation emotional, wondering why other people would question her faith. Following the drama in the house, Cates was visited by Chris Harrison, who told him his parents would be visiting and would have an opportunity to meet the women, something Cates was excited about because his parents' opinion is very important to him. When speaking with Harrison, Cates said he thinks his wife is there, but when asked if he wanted to take the step forward and introduce all the women to his parents, he said no. After letting the women know his parents would be visiting, he pulled Julia aside for a chat, letting her know it would be "cruel" for him to introduce her to his parents when he felt his romantic connection with the other women was stronger. "I just couldn't look at my mom and dad in the eye and say, ‘Hey, I could see Julia at the end of this,’" he told the women. "I didn't think it was fair to put her through that. I just want you all to know that you're all here because I do have feelings for each of you and I feel strongly enough that I want you to meet my parents." "I felt like she was a little more intense. That's just a little bit of a red flag for me," his dad said. "It's OK to be strong, Lord knows your mom is, and I love her for it, but there is a difference between being strong and being a little bit rigid and combative." Cates then let them know that he had noticed some of that behavior himself, noting that when everyone jumped in the pool a few days before, she refused and didn't want to get her hair wet, leading his mom to ask, "So why is she still here?" articles.title: Gérard Depardieu Rape Case Sent To Trial In Criminal Court After Actor Loses Appeal
articles.summary: Gérard Depardieu will stand trial in a criminal court on a rape charge related to accusations by actress Charlotte Arnould, after an appeal by his lawyers fa...
articles.body:
Gérard Depardieu will stand trial in a criminal court on a rape charge related to accusations by actress Charlotte Arnould, after an appeal by his lawyers failed.

The Paris Court of Appeal said on Thursday that Depardieu would be tried for one part of the accusations levelled by Arnould against the actor.

The actress, whose father was an old friend of the actor, accuses Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her twice in his Paris mansion in the summer of 2018 after she went to him for acting advice.

The court has ruled that Depardieu will be tried for the first alleged rape on August 7, 2018, but not the second alleged rape on August 13, due to insufficient evidence.

The decision to proceed with the trail comes eight months after Depardieu was found guilty of sexual assault and given an 18-month suspended sentence related to events on the set of Jean Becker's The Green Shutters in 2021.

The acto r last week announced he was abandoning plans to appeal the sentence and issued a statement saying that he recognized his culpability and apologized for the hurt he had caused.

Just days after the letter was published, investigative newsite Mediapart published details of a fresh sexual assault and rape complaint against the actor related to events on the shoot of Guillaume Nicloux's Thalasso in 2018.

His 18-month suspended sentence related to assaults on two female crew members on the set of The Green Shutters .

A number of women, who were not pressing charges, also gave evidence at the trial, including an actress who alleged Depardieu had shoved his hands into her knickers during a photo-call on the set of Netflix show Marseille .

Arnould was the first woman to pursue Depardieu in the courts in relation to sexual assault allegations, but her move came against a backdrop of growing rumors around the actor's sexually inappropriate treatment of female extras and crew members on film sets.

Her complaint was initially dismissed by the courts following a nine-month investigation for lack of evidence, but she filed a second complaint as a civil party, which resulted in an investigating judge being appointed in 2020, and Depardieu being indicted for rape and sexual assault in 2021.

In between times, Depardieu's public star plummeted following an exposé of his alleged sexual misconduct by state broadcaster channel France 2's investigative show Complément d'Enquête , entitled "The fall of the ogre", which aired in December 2023.

The allegations and 2026 guilty verdict have brought his acting career to a grinding halt. Since 2022, he has worked on only three productions, one of them directed by his longtime friend Fanny Ardant.

The criminal court is France's highest level of court reserved for crimes carrying sentences of more than five years, if the accused is found guilty.

articles.title: Khloé Kardashian admits she’s open to marrying gay man after 5 years without sex: ‘Depends what that gay man can do for me’
articles.summary: “Like, will you make me look pretty every day? Sold. That’s all it takes,” Kardashian said amid her celibacy journey.
articles.body:
Reality TV star Khloe Kardashian admitted she's open to marrying a gay man after five years of celibacy.

Kardashian and influencer Colt Paulsen discussed "lavender marriage" on The Kardashians .

"I mean, it depends what that gay man can do for me. Like, will you make me look pretty every day?" she asked.

Khloé Kardashian (maybe) wants a lavender kind of love!

After revealing earlier this month that she's demisexual amid a five-year celibacy journey, the reality TV icon said she's open to marrying a gay man 10 years after her divorce from Lamar Odom and five years after splitting from ex-boyfriend Tristan Thompson.

"You need a man, all your sisters are dating," influencer Colt Paulsen told Kardashian on the latest episode of Hulu's The Kardashians series.

He then suggested, "You can always do the lavender marriage. If you ever need, I'm here," to which Kardashain replied, "Oh, yeah. Well, that? I'm down with anytime!"

The show then defined via title card what exactly a "lavender marriage" is, with the program's text describing it as "a marriage of convenience between a man and a woman where one or both is queer."

In a confessional, the 42-year-old elaborated on her thoughts about lavender marriages — including if one would ever be the right fit for her at this stage of her life while raising two children.

"Would I have a lavender marriage? There's times, yes, and then other times, I'm like, to take care of one more person? I don't know," she admitted.

She continued: "I mean, it depends what that gay man can do for me. Like, will you make me look pretty every day? Sold. That's all it takes!"

Kardashian and Odom divorced in 2016 after seven years of marriage, while the dissolution of her relationship with Thompson led to her ongoing celibacy journey.

On a recent episode of her Khloé in Wonder Land podcast, Kardashian came to the realization that she's demisexual , which means that a person can only achieve physical intimacy after establishing an emotional connection with another person.

articles.title: Kelsey Grammer calls American Dream a ‘gift’ he wants to pass down to his 8 children
articles.summary: Kelsey Grammer says the American Dream is a "gift" that he wants to pass down to his eight children as he marks the United States' 250th anniversary with "The America Opus."
articles.body: Kelsey Grammer believes the American Dream is alive and well, and the "Frasier" star is determined to make sure his eight children understand the freedom and opportunity that come with it. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 71-year-old actor reflected on the values he hopes to instill in his children as the United States of America celebrates its 250th anniversary, and he helps commemorate the nation's history through the collector's book "The America Opus." "The thing I most want to pass down to them is the understanding that it's your job. Your gift is the American Dream," Grammer said. "What it entails is up to you." KELSEY GRAMMER WARNS OF CHILLING DANGER FACING AMERICANS WHO FORGET NATION'S FOUNDING HISTORY "Every individual has the same right to figure out what that dream is and to make it happen," he added. The "Cheers" alum shared his view that the American Dream is not just about achieving personal success, but also about having the opportunity to make a difference. WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER ON WHAT HE WANTS HIS 8 CHILDREN TO LEARN: 'YOUR GIFT IS THE AMERICAN DREAM' Grammer pointed to Alexander Graham Bell as an example of someone who made his American Dream a reality while helping others, noting that the inventor's efforts to help deaf children communicate eventually led to the development of the telephone. "My hat is off to people who end up thinking of something that millions of people need. Why wouldn't we allow those people success? Why wouldn't we praise them? Sort of laud them as being the examples of how wonderful America is," Grammer said. "These people are all American heroes by virtue of the fact that they kept working at their dream," he continued. "Their dream was to help somebody. And it ended up helping millions of people." When asked how he hopes his children will remember him beyond his Hollywood career, Grammer emphasized the importance of setting an example through hard work and personal responsibility. THE FOUNDING FATHERS GAVE US AMERICA. 250 YEARS LATER, WE STILL DEPEND ON GOOD DADS "I hope they look on me as a guy who was incredibly fair. Firm. I have high expectations of people, I expect people to show up," he said. "Because I do. One of my sayings that I say to people is like, if I've got a job being done around the house and I haven't seen the guys for a few weeks, I say, 'You know, if I did my job this way, I wouldn't have this house, I wouldn't have anything else.' "You gotta show up," Grammer continued. "That's the big thing. Your American Dream actually is in your hands. I mean, and I do say this to a lot of people these days, I say like, 'Anybody tells you the American Dream's over, don't give them your vote because that's what they want. They want it over. Theirs is that it's over.' You know, no thanks." Grammer, who has been married four times, shares his eldest child, daughter Spencer Grammer, 43, with his first wife, Doreen Alderman. He is also father to daughter Greer Grammer, 34, whom he shares with his ex-girlfriend Barrie Buckner. The "Grand Isle" actor has daughter Mason Olivia, 25, and son Jude Gordon, 22, with his ex-wife Camille Grammer, 54. He married British former flight attendant Kayte Walsh in 2011. Grammer and Walsh are parents to daughter Faith Evangeline, 14, and sons Kelsey Gabriel, 12, Auden James, 10, and Christopher, 1. 'MELROSE PLACE' STAR ANDREW SHUE SAYS 70% BELIEVE THE AMERICAN DREAM IS 'DEAD OR DYING' While speaking with Fox News Digital, Grammer, who previously indicated that he has considered running for office, said that for now, he had set aside his political ambitions to focus on fatherhood. "I have put it on the back burner because I've got all these new kids and I really want to be a present dad," he said. Grammer admitted that he has regrets over not being present enough for his older children earlier in their lives. WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER REFLECTS ON 250 YEARS OF U.S. HISTORY IN NEW BOOK 'AMERICA OPUS' "My first couple of kids — I wasn't around for them as much as I would have liked to have been," he said. "And I think they may even still have some sensibilities about that, sensitivity about it, rather, and I'd like to make it up to everybody because you need a dad there." Grammer went to say that he didn't have an understanding of what fatherhood meant after growing up without his own dad. The actor's parents, Frank Allen Grammer Jr. and Sally Cranmer Grammer, divorced when he was 2 years old, and he was raised primarily by his mother and maternal grandparents. In 1968, Grammer's father was shot and killed in the U.S. Virgin Islands when the actor was just 13. "I didn't have a dad, you know, I didn't know what it was to be called a dad till I was one," he said. "I'd never used the word till I became a dad. So it's really important to me, but a good dad, hopefully, would be what you want in office. You want a guy that shows up." Grammer also explained how he believes he has changed after becoming a father again later in life. "I've got four kids with my current wife, Kate, and it's such an extraordinary experience," he said. "It's just that — it's so lovely in every way. These surprising young human beings that are in your life and in your care, and you're gonna do your best to not mess them up, but we always do." "Kind of not really — I mean, look, I'm steady," he continued. "I'm a steady guy. Maybe I wasn't always, but I am now, and I'm proud of that and that they have that to look to." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS The six-time Emmy Award-winner went on to share the biggest lesson that he had learned about love and marriage after more than 15 years with Walsh. "Just stay in it," he said. "You just stay, you know, stay, work it out. I mean, Kate's a particularly level-headed woman." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "I always think of that song, Cat Stevens' song, 'I'm looking for a hard-headed woman,'" Grammer continued. "One that will make me do my best. She's the kind of person you want to do your best for. And so I'm here." Grammer recently teamed up with British luxury publisher Opus to create "The America Opus," a large-format illustrated book celebrating the United States' 250th anniversary. "The America Opus" explores pivotal moments in American history, highlighting the people, achievements and challenges that have shaped the country over the past two and a half centuries. "The America Opus" will be released in two editions, including the Marquee Edition, which is limited to 2,500 copies at $2,500, and a smaller Classic Edition with fewer pages. "What's nice about the book is we're not actually out to — we have no axe to grind or no political stance to make," Grammer said. "We're actually basically just doing some snapshots of extraordinary moments in the American story." "Some of them when we were in the ascendancy. Some of them maybe not our best story, not our best foot forward, but you know what, we're pretty open and honest about all that," Grammer continued. "But there's no reflection other than the fact that this has been an extraordinary experiment, the American experiment," he added. "And the 250 years that we've lived will hopefully point to another 250 that are just as extraordinary." "The America Opus," which is available for preorder and is expected to begin shipping in December, features an introduction by Grammer and a foreword by President Donald Trump, who also signed it. "I've never known a guy who loves America more than him," Grammer said of Trump. "But I will say this, if Kamala Harris had been the president when we were doing this book, we would have asked her to write a foreward and sign it because it's about the sitting president of the United States during the 250th birthday." articles.title: Before Sai Pallavi's casting as Sita sparked criticism, Shobhna Samarth called the 'OG Sita' by granddaughter Kajol faced backlash for playing the goddess while being eight months pregnant in 'Raambaan'
articles.summary: Long before Sai Pallavi's casting as Sita in Nitesh Tiwari's 'Ramayana' sparked discussions, another actress faced severe criticism for playing the
articles.body: Long before Sai Pallavi's casting as Sita in Nitesh Tiwari's 'Ramayana' sparked discussions, another actress faced severe criticism for playing the revered character on screen. Shobhna Samarth, whom her granddaughter Kajol has fondly referred to as the 'OG Sita', found herself at the centre of a controversy during the making of the 1948 film 'Raambaan'. The reason was that she was eight months pregnant while portraying the goddess.The issue drew a particularly sharp response from FilmIndia editor Baburao Patel, who objected to Shobhna playing Sita while expecting a child. In his review of the film, Patel argued that her pregnancy was incompatible with the idealised image of the goddess."Her pregnancy stares everyone in the eye and becomes a sickly and sacrilegious spectacle through 14147 feet of the film. It is contrary to the spirit of loftiness and sublimity associated with the name of Sita to ask a woman in her dangerously delicate situation to play a role which is worshipped by millions as the noblest and divine ideal of a woman," he wrote.Patel's criticism also extended to Shobhna's appearance. He questioned whether she was suited to portray Sita, making pointed remarks about her age and physical features."Apart from this problem of pregnancy, Shobhna, as the mother of several children, looks too old and emaciated a woman, with sunken cheeks, bulging anaemic eyes, shapeless arms and sagging hips to portray Sita," he added.The review went beyond criticising the casting, with Patel even urging Hindu audiences to boycott the film. He maintained that showing a visibly pregnant Shobhna as Sita could give young viewers the impression that the goddess was pregnant during her exile.The controversy was especially striking given the actress's earlier success in the role. Shobhna had first portrayed Sita in Vijay Bhatt's 'Bharat Milap' (1942), which depicted the events surrounding Ram, Sita and Lakshman's exile from Ayodhya. Following the film's success, Bhatt reunited the cast for 'Ram Rajya' in 1943, which further cemented Shobhna's association with the character.'Ram Rajya' also holds a notable place in Indian cinema history. Mahatma Gandhi, who was known to have little interest in films, is believed to have watched Vijay Bhatt's film, making it the only movie he saw during his lifetime.However, the same success did not follow with 'Raambaan', which arrived in 1948. The film traced the events leading up to Sita's abduction by Ravana, including Lakshman's encounter with Shurpanakha and Ram and Lakshman's alliance with Hanuman and Sugriva.Despite having earned recognition for her earlier portrayals of Sita, Shobhna's casting in 'Raambaan' became a subject of intense debate, with her pregnancy drawing criticism that went far beyond a discussion of her performance.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Priyanka Chopra pays tribute to the victims and martyrs of the 26/11 Mumbai attacks: 'Remembering the lives lost and the heroes who gave everything on 26/11'
articles.summary: Priyanka Chopra and Bhumi Pednekar have paid emotional tributes to the victims and brave defenders of the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks on its anniversary.
articles.body: Priyanka Chopra and Bhumi Pednekar have paid emotional tributes to the victims and brave defenders of the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks on its anniversary. While Priyanka shared a short note on Instagram, Bhumi spoke to the media about the strength and unity of the nation.Priyanka Chopra's Instagram tributePriyanka Chopra honoured the lives lost and the security personnel who risked everything to protect citizens. She posted on her Instagram Stories, "Remembering the lives lost and the heroes who gave everything on 26/11."Bhumi Pednekar calls it an attack on IndiaBhumi Pednekar, who was born in Mumbai, described the day in 2008 as "a dark day which halted the city". The 'Dum Laga Ke Haisha' actress thanked those who stood firm during the crisis and said the city holds a special place in her heart.The 'Pati Patni Aur Woh' star said, “I would like to say that all our martyrs, Mumbai police officers, our armed forces, survivors, frontline responders, and all the citizens of Mumbai who have spent such a dark day, and I am also from Mumbai, I was born here, I have Mumbai in my heart. I think the attack on 26/11 was not only on Mumbai, but on our country”.Bhumi also spoke about the spirit of the country and the importance of remembering those affected. She added, “But the most beautiful thing about our country is that wherever we see hatred, we will turn it into love; we will turn it into hope. And even today, where we remember all those martyrs, we remember all those people who lost their lives, their families, I bow my head and say that your stories, what happened to you, will never be forgotten. And we will fill the world with so much love that there will be no place for hatred. There will be no space for terrorism in the world."What happened on November 26, 2008On that day, ten Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists based in Pakistan carried out coordinated strikes across Mumbai. Their targets included the Taj Hotel, the Oberoi, CST, Leopold Cafe and Nariman House, among other places. The siege lasted 60 hours and left 166 people dead and 238 injured.Security forces killed nine of the ten attackers. articles.summary: Gerard Depardieu will stand trial in the alleged 2018 rape of Charlotte Arnould, who says the French actor assaulted her in his Paris home when she was 22.
articles.body: French actor Gerard Depardieu will stand trial in the alleged 2018 rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters Thursday. Arnould accused the 77-year-old Depardieu of raping her in 2018 when she was 22 and he was 70. She claims he assaulted her in his Paris home. Depardieu, a veritable star of French cinema, has faced numerous sexual assault claims in recent years. In May 2025, a Paris court found him guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set and ordered that he be added to France's national sex offender registry. CATE BLANCHETT MOURNS HOW #METOO GOT 'KILLED VERY QUICKLY,' STILL 'SYSTEMIC LAYER OF ABUSE' Depardieu initially appealed the ruling, but dropped his appeal in mid-November. "I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that no longer exists," he said, adding, "I have therefore decided to withdraw my appeal." Depardieu also apologized and said, "On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did." Despite appearing to acknowledge his behavior was inappropriate in the 2025 case, Depardieu has denied any wrongdoing in the Arnould case. GERARD DEPARDIEU SPEAKS OUT, MAINTAINS INNOCENCE AFTER BEING CHARGED FOR RAPE AND SEXUAL ASSAULT In a 2023 op-ed in French newspaper Le Figaro, Depardieu wrote, "Never, ever have I abused a woman. To harm a woman would be like kicking my own mother in the stomach." In the essay, he claimed, "A woman came to my house once, walking lightly, going up to my room of her own accord. She now says she was raped there. She returned there a second time. There has never been any coercion, violence, or protest between us." Arnould, in a social media post shortly after the letter became public, called it "a truly vile message." "He positions himself as the victim to elicit compassion and sow doubt. To put things in context, when I went to his place, I was 22 years old, I weighed 37 kilos because I suffered from anorexia, and he was a friend of my father's," she told Elle magazine. The young actress and aspiring dancer also added that "at no point did I consent." Arnould's attorney, Carine Durrieu-Diebolt, also said that she was "shocked and scandalized" at Depardieu's letter. Delphine Meillet, another attorney representing Depardieu, told The Associated Press that he disputes the ruling to proceed with his case, though he did not specify if he plans to appeal. Attorneys for Depardieu and Arnould did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment. You want to do it real, you want everything to be real, but then … That was the most vulnerable I’ve ever been."

articles.title: 'One Job Away' campaign is helping SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to keep health insurance
articles.summary: Actor Cheyenne Jackson’s “One Job Away" campaign helping fellow SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to maintain health insurance
articles.body: A grassroots social media campaign led by actor and singer Cheyenne Jackson has helped fellow SAG-AFTRA members struggling during declining film and TV production earn enough to keep their union health insurance. Jackson, known for his roles in "American Horror Story," "30 Rock" and "Glee," launched the "One Job Away" movement on Instagram last month to spotlight fellow performers struggling to earn enough to maintain medical coverage through the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. SAG-AFTRA requires members to earn at least $28,000 annually to qualify for health insurance, with four quarterly deadlines for meeting that threshold, depending on when they joined the union. NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE' For actors working job to job, meeting that requirement has become increasingly difficult as U.S. film and TV production contracts and healthcare costs rise. "So the success of the project so far at last count is that eight actors have been hired directly and at least 12 to 15 have been pinned or called back or gotten really close," Jackson told Fox News Digital. He described an overwhelming response, including hundreds of direct messages from actors hoping to be featured, many of whom are just a few hundred dollars short of qualifying. Among them is William Ngo, who was born and raised in Southern California but relocated to Philadelphia after work dried up following the pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike. Ngo, whose credits include The CW’s "The Vampire Diaries," HBO Max’s "The Staircase" and Apple’s "Bad Monkey," is just $500 short of qualifying for SAG-AFTRA health insurance. Actress and stunt performer Marie Gibeault, whose credits include Netflix’s "The Four Seasons" and multiple commercials, is only $800 short of qualifying. Navy veteran, actor and voice-over artist Jonathan Medina needs one guest role to qualify by the end of the year. ROB RIGGLE SAYS HOLLYWOOD WORK IS DISAPPEARING FROM LA: 'IT'S THE EXCEPTION NOW' Actor Alejandro Cardenas reached out to thank Jackson after the campaign helped him book a small role that put him over the earnings threshold. "After Cheyenne posted my picture and info, an executive from Lionsgate and friend of mine immediately called me and set me up into this job so I could make the money needed to reach the minimum to qualify for my health insurance again," Cardenas told Fox News Digital from the set he was working on in New Jersey. The actors’ profiles share a common thread: dwindling opportunities in Hollywood during fewer scripted television orders, increased cost-cutting and the continued shift of production elsewhere. TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS Jackson previously described the industry’s struggles as "systemic" during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. "People that have been leads of television shows have worked for years and years and years, and you know their faces, and you know their work. This year, they’re like, ‘What am I going to do?’" he said. Meanwhile, beginning Jan. 1, quarterly premiums and earnings thresholds are expected to rise by 1%, with additional annual increases of 1% to follow, according to terms negotiated in SAG-AFTRA’s latest contract with streamers and studios. A petition calling for an audit of the union’s health plan has also gained traction among members. SAG-AFTRA, which represents approximately 170,000 media professionals worldwide, has faced criticism over the nearly $1.1 million annual salary of its national executive director and chief negotiator, Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, as members struggle financially. Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA’s chief communications and marketing officer, Pamela Greenwalt, for comment. In response, a union representative provided a healthcare fact sheet and a membership termination sheet. Jackson, who also performs onstage, has expressed a desire to discuss how the system works, noting that actors can have a strong earnings year followed by a lean one that leaves them ineligible for health benefits. He told Fox News Digital that launching "One Job Away" was a way to pass along kindness he had received. Last year, for the first time in his 20-year career, Jackson found himself $6,000 short of meeting the health insurance eligibility requirements. Actress Kathy Bates, who had worked with him on "American Horror Story," arranged for him to have four speaking lines on her CBS series "Matlock." The work was enough to qualify him and his family for coverage. "I really did nothing," Jackson said of launching "One Job Away." He added that several peers, including actresses Jamie Lee Curtis and Sarah Paulson, have reached out to ask how they can help. articles.body: La gala de los Premios Ondas volvió a convertirse un año más en un escaparate para la ironía y la mirada crítica sobre el ecosistema mediático español. Entre aplausos y risas del público, Jordi Évole aprovechó el micrófono para lanzar un alegato en clave de humor sobre la relación entre la actualidad política, la televisión y las jornadas electorales, recordando que "El domingo hay unas elecciones y hay que ir a votar. Y yo sé el tipo de gente que se junta en los Ondas". Con ese punto de partida cómplice, el comunicador pidió a los asistentes que miraran más allá de la ceremonia y pensaran en el esfuerzo sostenido de determinados rostros de la comunicación. "Entonces, os quiero pedir que penséis en vuestros compañeros y compañeras que llevan cuatro años dándolo todo para que caiga este Gobierno", señaló, invitando a la sala a poner nombres y apellidos a esa idea. En su enumeración, Évole citó de forma directa a figuras muy reconocidas del panorama mediático y de la tertulia política. "Pensad en ellos, que se os pase por la cabeza, yo qué sé, Iker (Jiménez), Pablo (Motos), Antonio (Ferreras), Carmen (Porter), Ana Rosa (Quintana)... pensad en todos ellos y sobre todo también pensad en Eduardo Inda. Acordaros de él el domingo". El tono satírico alcanzó su punto culminante cuando el presentador vinculó el resultado de las urnas con el estado de ánimo de esos comunicadores al día siguiente. "No les demos un mal lunes. Esta gente lleva mucho tiempo dándolo todo para que esto cambie. No les demos un mal lunes, por favor", añadió ante la reacción de los presentes. Évole cerró su intervención con una frase de aparente recomendación que arrancó una reacción en el auditorio, resumiendo con sorna el espíritu de su mensaje. "El domingo si os podéis quedar en casa, mejor. ¡Venga! ¡Hostia, sí se puede!", remató el periodista para concluir su intervención.
